judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard claims-made legend whose terms ('first made', 'reported in writing ... pursuant to the terms herein') are defined or cross-referenced elsewhere, leaving little in the wording itself to construe. The only softness is that it summarises rather than states the operative trigger.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is a declarations legend that defers to Section I and Section V.A, but it says nothing about claims relating back under the Awareness Provision (VI.A) or the interrelated-acts deeming in V.A, so an insured could read the legend as the whole trigger. That gap is a modest, not a squarely contradictory, one.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The item is captioned 'Item $6' while the same page already carries an Item 6 (Punitive Damages), and the ERP premium is stated only as '125 percent of annualized premium' without saying of which year — a mechanical numbering/expression defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section II.C expressly conditions the ERP on 'the additional premium required by the Insurer in Item 5(A) in the Declarations', so a Declarations item numbered 6 leaves the cross-reference hanging. That mismatch with II.C is a genuine, if curable, internal inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short attestation; 'another duly authorized representative' is slightly loose but the signature requirement is plain on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the Declarations and does not bear on the operative coverage sections; nothing in VIII.K (Alteration and Assignment), which also requires an authorized representative's signature, contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional consideration/reliance recital; 'all information provided to the Insurer' is broad but is picked up by the defined term Application.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It points the same way as VIII.B (Representations and Severability) and III.A (Application), though it recites reliance in absolute terms while VIII.B severs imputation among Insured Individuals — a recital-versus-operative tension that is mild.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reporting condition combines a vague standard ('as soon as practicable after any Insured first becomes aware') with a hard sixty-day outer limit, and 'a Wrongful Act which takes place before or during the Policy Period' invites argument about retroactive reach; these are the classic construction points in a claims-made-and-reported policy.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The outer limit of sixty days after expiry of the Policy Period sits awkwardly with VI.C, which allows notice of a Claim arising from a noticed Potential Claim within sixty days after that Claim is first made (potentially long after expiry), and with V.A's deeming of Claims to a prior policy. Those relationships give a court real work to do.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The spousal extension is carefully bounded by two enumerated bases and an express carve-out for the spouse's own wrongful acts, with 'spouse' expressly extended to domestic partners.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It tracks the definitions of Loss (III.L) and Insured Individual (III.J) without adding the spouse as an Insured, and I found no provision pulling the other way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, standard estates/representatives extension with an express exclusion for the representatives' own wrongdoing; nothing lexically open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with III.I/III.J and with VIII.I (Bankruptcy), which likewise contemplates insolvent insureds; no conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The ERP trigger ('if the Insurer chooses not to renew or the Parent Company cancels') is an exclusive-seeming list that omits insurer cancellation for non-payment, and the sentence that a Claim made in the ERP 'shall be deemed to have been made during the immediately preceding Policy Period' sits oddly beside the requirement that it be first made during the ERP.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to Item 5(A) while the Declarations caption reads Item 6, and its deeming rule must be reconciled with Section I's sixty-day reporting cap and V.A's statement that coverage applies only to Claims deemed first made during the Policy Period. Those are specific, checkable frictions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'any other such documents submitted in connection with the underwriting' is an open-ended catch-all appended to enumerated specifics, and the sweep into publicly filed DOL/EEOC documents is unusually broad.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: VIII.B makes 'all such statements' the basis of the Policy and incorporates them, so the breadth of Application matters elsewhere; but nothing in VIII.B contradicts this definition outright.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The inclusive limb ('any other payment to or for the benefit of an employee arising out of the employment relationship') is very broad and its second sentence carving out salary, wages and commissions creates a boundary a court could be asked to draw.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Benefits is used in Loss exclusions 4 and 6 and in Exclusion B.1, whose carve-back for 'any Claim for wrongful termination of employment' partly restores what Loss item 6 (severance) excludes; that interaction is a real, if secondary, tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One line reaching 'oral, written or implied' contracts; 'implied employment contract' is a term whose boundary is genuinely contestable, though the drafting is deliberate and broad.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion A.4 and B.3 cut back contract-based recoveries, so the broad grant here is qualified rather than contradicted; the carve-backs ('would have been liable in the absence of such contract') keep them reconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is the coverage trigger term and the enumerated limbs — 'a written demand ... for monetary or non-monetary relief', an EEOC/OFCCP 'or a similar formal proceeding ... commenced by a notice of charges, formal investigative order or similar document' — combine specific instances with catch-alls whose reach is genuinely contestable, and the exclusion for collective-bargaining proceedings sharpens the line.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Whether a given communication is a 'Claim' or only a 'Potential Claim' (III.R) determines the operation of VI.A and of V.A's rule deeming interrelated Claims first made under a prior policy, so the definition cannot be applied without reconciling those provisions. That is exactly where a claims-made dispute lands.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses' is a standard but genuinely elastic qualifier, though the parenthetical carve-out for wages and overhead is precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It dovetails with V.A (defence costs erode the Limit), V.C (no costs without consent) and IV.B (defence costs only); I found no contradiction among them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single broad sentence keyed to violations of statute, regulation, ordinance or common law 'concerning discrimination in employment', which is definite in kind even if wide in scope.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion A.5 removes many employment statutes but expressly preserves Retaliation claims and the Equal Pay Act, so the interaction is drafted rather than inconsistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list is mechanically broken (item 1 reads 'duly appointed officer' in the singular and the fifth limb has lost its number) and 'individuals whose labor or service is directed by the Policyholder' is a vague boundary for independent workers.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Employee overlaps but does not match Insured Individual (III.J), which requires a written indemnity agreement for leased workers and contractors, and III.V excludes independent-contractor claims from Third Party Claims — a set of relationships a court could be asked to harmonise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Limb 3, 'illegal work related harassment', is a residual catch-all sitting after two specific sexual-harassment limbs, and 'interferes with an Employee's performance' is an imprecise threshold.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Harassment feeds Wrongful Employment Act (III.X) and the Other Workplace Tort tail-condition; nothing elsewhere contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line composite definition with no elastic term of its own.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends entirely on III.J and III.O, which are themselves defined; no conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list is bounded and each limb carries its own condition, though 'volunteers whose labor or service is directed by the Policyholder' and the written-indemnity precondition leave some application questions.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits beside III.G (Employee), which covers leased workers and volunteers without the indemnity precondition, so who is an Insured versus a claimant Employee can require reconciliation. The mismatch looks deliberate rather than incoherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'common nexus any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction, cause or series of causally or logically connected facts' is famously elastic — 'logically connected' has no stated boundary and is precisely the kind of phrase parties read differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It drives V.A's single-Claim deeming and Exclusion A.2(b)'s prior-claim bar, so its reach decides whether a Claim belongs to this policy period at all; that dependency is where the incoherence risk lies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long definition with nine carve-outs; 'matters uninsurable under the law applicable to this Policy' and 'the multiple portion of any multiplied damage award' are open terms, and the drafting expressly includes front and back pay while excluding future salary.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Carve-out 3 (multiplied damages) sits against III.S, which brings ADEA/EPA/FMLA liquidated (double) damages into Punitive Damages, which Item 6 says are covered — a genuine internal pull. Exclusion B.1's Benefits carve-back adds a further interaction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The enumeration is mechanically corrupt (two limbs numbered 4, a limb numbered 8, a stray 'N.') and the closing 'but only when alleged as part of a Claim for' condition qualifies an entire list whose scope is thereby uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The tail condition ties it to Breach of Employment Contract, Discrimination, Harassment, Retaliation or Wrongful Job Action, all defined, and III.X refers to 'Other Workplace Torts' in the plural — a small definitional slippage rather than a conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure pointer to Item 1 of the Declarations with nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 1 identifies FINRA and the reference is consistent throughout (VII, VIII.A.2, VIII.J).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite; the debtor-in-possession inclusion is explicit.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It squares with VIII.A.2's statement that a debtor-in-possession status is not an acquisition and with VIII.I (Bankruptcy); no conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition itself is a pointer to Item 2, but it carries a cross-reference that appears mis-numbered, which is a mechanical defect on the face of the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Cancellation, the only source of 'prior termination', is in the General Conditions (VIII.C), whereas Section VI is the Awareness Provision, so the cross-reference to 'Section VI.C' points at a subsection about notice of subsequent Claims. That is a concrete misfit with VIII.C.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition piles catch-alls on catch-alls — 'any substance ... exhibiting any hazardous characteristics' and 'any other air emission, odor, ... noise' — so its outer boundary is contestable, though it is drafted to be all-embracing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Pollutants is used only in Exclusion A.7, which carves back Retaliation claims by Employees; nothing elsewhere pulls against it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'an allegation or accusation ... provided such allegation does not constitute a Claim, but subsequently may give rise to a Claim' is circular and its boundary against 'Claim' is genuinely hard to apply.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The line between Potential Claim and Claim (III.D) decides whether VI.A relation-back or the Section I reporting rule applies, so a court applying VI.A must construe both together. That interaction is specific and live.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite in form: punitive/exemplary damages plus named statutory liquidated damages.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Loss carve-out 3 excludes 'the multiple portion of any multiplied damage award', which is exactly what ADEA/FMLA liquidated damages are, while Item 6 elects Punitive Damages coverage — a real tension between III.S, III.L.3 and the Declarations.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'illegal retaliatory treatment of Employees, including any retaliatory treatment against an Employee for ...' uses an open 'including' before a specific list, leaving the residual scope of the general words uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Retaliation is the carve-back in Exclusions A.5 and A.7, so its breadth determines how much of the statutory exclusion survives; that is an interaction worth checking but not a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The trailing clause 'on or before the effective date of this Policy, or after the effective date ... if the entity is covered pursuant to Section VIII.A.1' is syntactically strained and its temporal limitation is hard to parse.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: VIII.A.1 deems an acquired entity a Subsidiary only if its employees are under ten percent of Employees, yet a later paragraph gives ninety days' cover where headcount grows by more than 110 percent, leaving a gap this definition does not address. Exclusion A.6 and VIII.A.3 also depend on it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'any natural person who is, or attempted to be, a customer or vendor' is loose, and the exclusion of independent-contractor claims cuts across the categories used elsewhere.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Third Party Claim coverage depends on Item 7 in the Declarations, whose box marking is not clearly legible, and III.G treats independent contractors as Employees while this definition excludes their claims — both connections could be argued.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line umbrella definition with nothing elastic in it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It simply aggregates III.X and III.Z; the only wrinkle is that Third Party Claim cover is conditional on Item 7 while Wrongful Act is unconditional, which the Insuring Agreement already handles.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'by any other persons for whom the Insureds are legally responsible' is an open-ended residual category, and the reference to 'Other Workplace Torts' does not match the defined singular term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on five defined terms and the Other Workplace Tort tail condition, which limits those torts to claims also alleging one of the same five categories — a circularity that is awkward but workable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Each limb turns on the word 'wrongful', which the Policy never defines, and 'deprivation of a career opportunity' and 'adverse change in the terms, conditions or status of employment' are notably open-textured.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds III.X and is qualified by Exclusion B.1's carve-back for wrongful termination; no direct conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list of protected bases ends with 'or on any other basis prohibited by law', a general catch-all after enumerated specifics, though the discrimination requirement narrows it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is operative only if Item 7 elects Third Party Claim coverage and pairs with III.V's exclusion of independent-contractor claims; consistent so far as I can see.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Several limbs combine enumerated statutes with residual sweeps — A.5's 'including any other federal, state local or foreign statute or law similar to any statute or law described in (a) through (h)' and A.11's 'including but not limited to' list — and A.12's 'if evidenced by ... a document or written statement by an Insured' is a notoriously contested formulation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A.5's carve-back for 'any Claim for Retaliation' has to be reconciled with III.T's broad Retaliation definition and with Insuring Agreement A, and A.8's mental-anguish proviso appears to swallow much of the exclusion it qualifies. Those are checkable frictions with III.T and Section I.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The lead-in ('the Insurer shall only pay Defense Costs, and not other components of Loss') plus B.4's sweep of 'any other equitable remedy' after enumerated forms of non-monetary relief creates a general-versus-specific question, and B.1's wrongful-termination carve-back is undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: B.1's carve-back restores Benefits in wrongful-termination claims while Loss items 4 and 6 exclude future wages and severance outright, so the two provisions must be harmonised. That is a specific, identifiable pull against III.L.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The relation-back rule — all Claims arising from the same or Interrelated Wrongful Acts deemed one Claim first made on the earlier of two dates — imports the elastic 'Interrelated Wrongful Acts' test and the further phrase 'valid notice ... under this Policy or any prior policy'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its closing sentence ('coverage applies only to Claims deemed first made during the Policy Period') has to be squared with II.C, which deems ERP Claims made in the preceding period, and with VI.A's relation-back of Potential Claims; those interactions are exactly what a claims-made fight turns on.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two lines pointing to Item 4; the only unstated point is how the single retention applies to Claims deemed one Claim.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with V.A's single-Claim deeming and V.C's fifty-percent-of-retention consent threshold it works, though a per-Claim retention plus deemed aggregation can raise a question. No direct contradiction found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It uses several standards courts routinely construe — consent 'not to be unreasonably withheld', Insureds who 'unreasonably refuse to consent', and a hammer clause — and combines a duty to defend with a bar on the Insureds incurring any Defense Costs without consent.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The duty to defend 'any Claim ... alleging a Wrongful Act' sits against IV.B, under which the Insurer pays only Defense Costs for certain claims, and against V.A's exhaustion rule; those provisions interlock but the defence duty's breadth versus the exclusions can be argued.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'becomes aware of a Potential Claim' and the deeming of any later Claim to 'the Policy Period in which the Potential Claim was first reported' are workable but depend on the circular Potential Claim definition; the last sentence's 'such circumstances' has no clear antecedent.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This relation-back cannot be squared easily with Section I's absolute bar on reporting more than sixty days after the Policy Period expires, nor with V.A's statement that coverage applies only to Claims deemed first made during the Policy Period. That is a specific, nameable tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It lists six specific contents for a Potential Claim notice and a residual duty to give 'such additional information and cooperation as it may reasonably require', made a condition precedent — the residual duty is open but reasonableness-bounded.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports VI.A and echoes the cooperation duty in V.C and the condition precedent in VIII.H; I found no provision that contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'as soon as practicable, but in no event later than sixty (60) days after such Claim is first made' is a definite outer limit paired with a soft standard, the usual formulation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its sixty-day clock runs from when the subsequent Claim is made, whereas Section I caps reporting at sixty days after the Policy Period expires, so a Claim maturing long after expiry is treated differently by the two provisions. That is a concrete conflict with the Insuring Agreement's proviso.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Notice is 'deemed to be received and effective upon actual receipt ... or one day following the date such notices are sent, whichever is earlier', which produces the odd result that notice can be effective before receipt, and the cross-reference reads 'Item 711'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 11 splits claim notices from all other notices, and Section I and VI impose the operative reporting deadlines, so the deeming rule here directly affects whether reporting was timely under those provisions. The mis-citation and the deeming rule together are worth checking against Item 11.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The paragraph is internally strained: entities become Subsidiaries only if their headcount is under ten percent, but the 'notwithstanding' paragraph gives ninety days' cover only where headcount grows above 110 percent, leaving the middle band unaddressed, and 'as for a period of ninety (90) days' is mangled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: III.U defines Subsidiary by reference back to this subsection and Exclusion A.6 denies cover for pre-acquisition acts, so the gap between the ten percent and 110 percent tests has to be resolved across three provisions. That is a genuine whole-instrument problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The change-of-control run-off is stated in definite terms with express carve-outs for receivership and debtor-in-possession status; little to construe lexically.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says coverage 'shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company', which qualifies VIII.C.1's unrestricted right of the Parent Company to cancel — a limited but identifiable tension. Otherwise it fits III.O and VIII.A.3.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two lines with a clear cut-off tied to the date the organisation ceased to be a Subsidiary; 'termination of the Policy' rather than 'Policy Period' is a small imprecision.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It complements Exclusion A.6 (no cover for acts while not a Subsidiary) and III.U; no contradiction located, though 'termination of the Policy' must be read with III.P.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All such statements are the basis of this Policy' combined with a severability regime and a broad imputation list (including 'human resources manager or risk manager') leaves scope for argument about whose knowledge counts, and the text is mechanically garbled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It incorporates the Application into the Policy while VIII.K declares the Policy the entire agreement, and III.A defines Application expansively — those three provisions have to be reconciled. A modest but real integration tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The enumeration is mechanically broken (items rendered as 'N', 'an', '8') and item 1 gives the Parent Company an unqualified right to cancel with no minimum notice.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the provision III.P's cross-reference should have pointed to, VIII.A.2 says coverage 'shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company' after a change of control, and II.C makes the ERP right depend on who cancels or non-renews. Those three connections give a court something to reconcile.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The excess wording is confined to 'Loss arising from any Third Party Claim' yet closes with 'in all other events, this Policy is intended to provide primary insurance', a sweeping residual whose reach against other insurance is debatable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Third Party Claim cover itself depends on Item 7 in the Declarations, so if that election is not clearly made the excess clause has no obvious field of operation; otherwise nothing contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, worldwide, with no qualifying language.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the worldwide references in III.F, III.Q and IV.A.11; no conflict found, though the currency clause (VIII.F) is its natural companion.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Specific conversion mechanic tied to a named publication and identified dates; nothing open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits VIII.E (Territory) and III.L (Loss) without friction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard subrogation with a broad cooperation duty ('everything necessary'), which is conventional rather than ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably with V.C's cooperation duty and VIII.H; no conflicting provision located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'full compliance with all the terms of this Policy' as a condition precedent is an absolute formulation that courts often have to soften or construe, though its meaning is plain on the page.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reinforces the condition-precedent language in VI.B and the notice provisions; nothing in the Policy contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, symmetrical bankruptcy clause with nothing elastic in the wording.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches III.O's inclusion of a debtor in possession and VIII.A.2's statement that receivership is not an acquisition; consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It appoints the Parent Company as agent for all notices with a parenthetical exception for 'the giving of notice to apply for any Extended Reporting Period', a carve-out whose practical operation is not spelled out.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: II.C says the ERP election notice is 'given by the Insured' and gives the right to the Policyholder or the Insured Individuals, so the carve-out here must be read with II.C and VII; that is a small but identifiable interaction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It combines a written-endorsement-only variation clause with an entire-agreement statement and a non-waiver clause, each in definite terms; the non-waiver sentence is oddly two-sided but clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The entire-agreement statement sits against VIII.B, which incorporates the Application and all submitted statements into the Policy, and against the Declarations and Item 12 endorsements — a nameable integration tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short interpretive rule stating headings form no part of the terms; nothing to construe in itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Several provisions are cross-referenced by section heading (for example III.P's reference to a lettered subsection), so disclaiming headings can complicate those references, but the clause is standard.
